title: England's schools are winning. Why are the experts so grumpy?
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman argues that England's steady 2025 PISA results, achieved while most of the OECD and EU slid, should be a cause for satisfaction, yet education professors in England were among the first to question the scores on technical grounds. He names Christian Bokhove, Ian Thompson and David Spendlove as examples of an establishment that downplays the result. His explanation is that the reforms behind England's relative success were carried out against sustained opposition from that same establishment. He offers an analogy: a government running a vaccination campaign against medical advice and then watching doctors dispute the improved figures. He contrasts Scotland and Wales, which followed the establishment and declined, and turns to Australia, where he sees the same deference in teacher registration and training rules. The piece closes with a call for policymakers to stop leaving education to its experts class and to follow England's lead with accountability and action.
points: Ashman reads the academic reaction to England's PISA result as a pattern of an establishment disputing success that came from reforms it opposed.
The vaccination analogy frames the dispute as experts questioning outcome data after their own advice was ignored.
Scotland and Wales are offered as cautionary cases of systems that listened to the establishment, downgraded content knowledge and diluted accountability.
In Australia he points to registration barriers for English-trained teachers and weaker compliance checks on teacher training as signs of the same problem.
His policy conclusion is to expand alternative routes into teaching, hold providers accountable on a regular inspection cycle, and put actions ahead of theory.
quotes: You might have thought that education professors in England who are responsible for education research and for training new teachers would allow themselves a moment of measured satisfaction. If so, you would have thought wrong.
Instead, they were some of the first to question the validity of England’s PISA scores on technical grounds.
The truth is that the reforms that probably helped England sustain its position were conducted against extreme and sustained opposition from England’s education establishment.

It would be like a government instituting a vaccination campaign against the advice of the medical establishment and then, when the campaign led to reduced levels of illness, the establishment would question these figures on technical grounds or argue that although people might be healthier, they are not necessarily any happier.
These essentially downgraded content knowledge, devolved decision making to hard-pressed schools and diluted accountability measures.
We should be doing the reverse of this and expanding alternative routes into teaching.
If we leave education to its experts class, we will not improve. There is no appetite for it. Policy must instead follow the lead of England.
We don’t need sermons. We don’t need to be spoken down to. We don’t need Romantic but unworkable theories. We need actions.
